title: REUBEN LOST HIS PREEMINENCE BECAUSE HE WENT UP TO HIS FATHER’S BED — AND ONE MOMENT OF SIN CHANGED HIS FAMILY’S FUTURE
paragraphs: REUBEN LOST HIS PREEMINENCE BECAUSE HE WENT UP TO HIS FATHER’S BED — AND ONE MOMENT OF SIN CHANGED HIS FAMILY’S FUTURE

He was born first. He had the birthright. He was supposed to lead. But one decision in a private place cost him something he could never recover. And what happened to Reuben carries a terrifying warning about hidden sin, a heartbreaking lesson about consequences, and a glorious revelation about the grace of Jesus Christ.
There are some mistakes you wish you could erase.
Not because anyone found out.
Not because you were embarrassed.
But because somewhere deep inside, you know that something changed the moment you crossed that line.

You remember who you were before it happened. You remember the convictions you once carried, the boundaries you promised yourself you would never cross, the prayers you prayed when your heart was still tender toward God.
And then came that moment.
A temptation you entertained too long. A desire you refused to surrender. A secret you convinced yourself would remain buried.
Perhaps nobody saw it.
Perhaps nobody confronted you.
Perhaps life continued as though nothing had happened.
But you knew.
And the question that keeps returning when the room becomes quiet is not simply, “Will anyone ever find out?”
It is something far more frightening.
“What have I lost because of what I allowed?”
If that question has ever haunted you, stay with this story.
Because thousands of years ago, a man named Reuben stood at the intersection of privilege, desire, consequence, and a future he could no longer control.
He was not an outsider trying to enter the family of promise.
He was already inside it.
He was the firstborn son of Jacob.
And that is what makes his story so devastating.
He did not have to steal his position.
He was born into it.
Genesis 29:32 tells us that Leah gave birth to a son and named him Reuben, saying, “Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me.” (KJV)
His name, רְאוּבֵן (Reʾuven), is traditionally connected with the Hebrew expression רְאוּ בֵן (reʾu ven), meaning “See, a son!”
Before Reuben ever understood his own name, his birth had already become part of his mother’s longing to be seen and loved.
Imagine that.
A child entering the world carrying the hopes of a wounded woman.

Leah was not the wife Jacob had originally wanted. Genesis tells us that Jacob loved Rachel more than Leah. In that painful family situation, Leah hoped the birth of her first son might finally bring her the affection she desired.
Reuben began his life surrounded by complicated relationships, rivalry, and emotional wounds he did not create.
Yet none of those circumstances excused what he would later choose.
And none of them canceled the extraordinary privilege attached to his position.

In the ancient family structure reflected in the biblical narrative, the firstborn son ordinarily possessed special rights of inheritance and family standing. Deuteronomy 21:17 later identifies the firstborn’s right to a double portion of inheritance.
Reuben was Jacob's firstborn.
The natural expectation was that he would occupy a place of distinction among his brothers.
Then something happened that Scripture records with almost unbearable brevity.
Genesis 35:22 says:
“And it came to pass, when Israel dwelt in that land, that Reuben went and lay with Bilhah his father's concubine: and Israel heard it.” (KJV)
Read that last sentence again.
“And Israel heard it.”
No lengthy explanation.
No attempt to soften what happened.
No elaborate account of Reuben's motives.
Just the terrible fact that he had sexual relations with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and his father learned of it.
Bilhah was not a stranger to this household. She had been Rachel's servant and had borne Jacob two sons, Dan and Naphtali.
This was not merely an inappropriate romantic encounter. It was a grave violation of the family relationship, involving his father's concubine and dishonoring his father's household.

The text does not tell us whether Reuben was driven by lust, resentment, rivalry, or an attempt to assert status. Some interpreters have suggested possible motives, but Scripture does not explicitly identify one.
We must not pretend to know what God has not revealed.
What Scripture does reveal is sufficient.
Reuben crossed a boundary he had no right to cross.
And the consequences did not disappear simply because the account moved on.
That is one of the most sobering realities in the entire story.
Sometimes the consequences of sin do not arrive immediately.
Sometimes the morning after looks strangely ordinary.
The sun rises.
People continue working.
Meals are prepared.
Conversations happen.
Years pass.
And a person begins to imagine that because judgment has not fallen, the matter has somehow ceased to matter.
But silence is not the same as innocence.
And delay is not the same as divine approval.
Ecclesiastes 8:11 warns that when judgment against evil is not executed quickly, human hearts can become emboldened to continue in wrongdoing.
Perhaps you know something about that dangerous silence.
You crossed a boundary once, and nothing seemed to happen.
So you crossed it again.
You told yourself that because you were still functioning, still attending church, still serving, still receiving compliments, everything must be fine.
But outward activity is not proof that inward compromise is harmless.
A person can continue performing religious duties while desperately needing repentance.
A person can speak about holiness while privately negotiating with sin.
A person can be surrounded by people and still be hiding from the truth.
And one of the enemy's most destructive lies is that what happens in secret can never touch what God has entrusted to you.
Years later, as Jacob approached death, he gathered his sons and spoke words concerning their futures.
Then he addressed Reuben.
Listen carefully to Genesis 49:3–4:
“Reuben, thou art my firstborn, my might, and the beginning of my strength, the excellency of dignity, and the excellency of power:
Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel; because thou wentest up to thy father's bed; then defiledst thou it: he went up to my couch.” (KJV)
Can you imagine hearing those words from your dying father?
“Thou art my firstborn.”
For one brief moment, Reuben hears his original dignity acknowledged.
“My might.”
“The beginning of my strength.”
“The excellency of dignity.”
“The excellency of power.”
Everything sounds like the beginning of a magnificent blessing.
Then comes the sentence that changes everything.
“Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel.”
In Hebrew, the opening expression of Genesis 49:4 is:
פַּחַז כַּמַּיִם אַל־תּוֹתַר
Paḥaz kammayim, ʾal-totar.
The phrase describes Reuben as reckless or turbulent like water, followed by the declaration that he would not retain preeminence.
The Hebrew word פַּחַז (paḥaz) conveys a sense of recklessness, instability, or uncontrolled impetuosity.
The verb connected with totar carries the idea of being left over, exceeding, or having superiority in this context.
Jacob's words are therefore not merely a criticism of Reuben's personality.
They announce the loss of his superior standing.
The man who began with the privilege of being firstborn would not retain the preeminence normally associated with that position.
And Jacob explicitly connected that loss with Reuben's defilement of his father's bed.
There is something deeply unsettling about the way the passage moves from dignity to disgrace.
Jacob did not deny that Reuben was his firstborn.
He did not erase his identity as his son.
But he did announce that Reuben's conduct had affected his standing.
That distinction matters.
Because sometimes we want forgiveness to mean that every consequence must disappear.
We want repentance to rewind the clock.
We want grace to make the past as though it never happened in every earthly sense.
But the Bible never promises that every consequence of sin will be removed in this life.
A betrayed spouse may forgive, yet rebuilding trust can take years.
A parent may repent of harsh words, yet still need to patiently repair a wounded relationship.
A believer may receive God's mercy while facing the results of financial dishonesty, sexual misconduct, or other destructive decisions.
Forgiveness is real.
Restoration is possible.
But grace does not require us to pretend that sin never caused damage.
And Reuben's story refuses to let us confuse the two.
First Chronicles 5:1 makes the consequence unmistakable:

“Now the sons of Reuben the firstborn of Israel, (for he was the firstborn; but, forasmuch as he defiled his father's bed, his birthright was given unto the sons of Joseph the son of Israel: and the genealogy is not to be reckoned after the birthright.” (KJV)
There it is.
Written into the historical record.
He was the firstborn.
But because he defiled his father's bed, his birthright was given to Joseph's sons.
The Hebrew word בְּכֹרָה (bekhorah) means “birthright,” referring here to the special privilege associated with firstborn status.
Reuben's biological position remained a historical fact.
His birthright privilege did not.
First Chronicles 5:2 adds another important detail:
“For Judah prevailed above his brethren, and of him came the chief ruler; but the birthright was Joseph's.” (KJV)
Notice how carefully Scripture distinguishes these developments.
The birthright went to Joseph, represented in the inheritance arrangements through his sons Ephraim and Manasseh.
The line of rulership was associated with Judah.
Reuben did not simply lose everything to one brother.
The privileges that might naturally have been expected to accompany his firstborn position were distributed elsewhere in God's unfolding purposes.
Joseph received the birthright.
Judah became the royal line.
And from Judah, in the fullness of biblical history, would come the Messiah.
But before we rush to the hope of that revelation, we need to face the warning.
Because Reuben's downfall confronts a dangerous assumption many believers carry without realizing it.
We assume that because God has given us something, our conduct cannot affect our stewardship of it.
We assume spiritual privilege makes us immune to spiritual consequences.
We assume that because we know Scripture, we cannot become enslaved to what Scripture condemns.
We assume that because God has used us before, He must approve of everything we are doing now.
But privilege is not permission.
Calling is not a license for compromise.
And knowing the truth is not the same as obeying it.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 10:12:
That warning is not meant to drive us into hopelessness.
It is meant to destroy spiritual arrogance.
The person who believes he is incapable of falling may already be neglecting the vigilance that faith requires.
And sometimes the most dangerous sentence a believer can say is, “I would never do that.”
Peter once spoke with extraordinary confidence about his loyalty to Jesus.
Yet before the rooster crowed, he denied knowing his Lord three times.
David was a king who had received extraordinary promises from God, yet his sin involving Bathsheba brought devastating consequences.
Samson possessed remarkable strength, yet his repeated compromises led him into captivity and humiliation.
These accounts are not identical to Reuben's story, and we must not flatten their differences.
But together they testify to one enduring truth.
No human being becomes spiritually safe by trusting in personal strength.
We need the sustaining grace of God.
We need humility.
We need obedience.
We need to flee temptation rather than entertain it.
And we need to stop calling dangerous compromises harmless simply because they have become familiar.
Perhaps this is where the story becomes painfully personal.
Because you may not have committed Reuben's particular sin.
You may never have defiled your father's bed.
But perhaps there is a boundary you know you have crossed.
A conversation that became too intimate.
A relationship you kept secret.
A screen you returned to when everyone else was asleep.
A lie you maintained because the truth would cost you something.
A bitterness you continued feeding long after God called you to forgive.
A private habit you have learned to defend rather than surrender.
And perhaps the most frightening part is not that you fell.
It is that you have begun to feel comfortable where you once felt convicted.
If that describes you, please hear this carefully.
The answer is not to sink deeper into shame.
The answer is to return to God in repentance.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
Not some unrighteousness.
All unrighteousness.
But confession is not an attempt to manipulate God into approving what we refuse to leave.
Genuine repentance involves turning toward God and away from sin.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated “repentance,” refers to a change of mind and disposition that, in biblical usage, involves a genuine turning toward God.
Repentance is more than being embarrassed that someone discovered the truth.
It is more than regretting the consequences.
It is more than crying because something precious was lost.
It is recognizing sin for what it is and turning to the mercy of God.
And this is where Reuben's story becomes even more heartbreaking.
Because Scripture does not portray him as a man without any evidence of conscience or concern.
In Genesis 37, when Reuben's brothers plotted against Joseph, Reuben attempted to prevent Joseph's death.
Genesis 37:21–22 records that he urged them not to kill Joseph and intended to rescue him and return him to their father.
Later, when Reuben discovered that Joseph was gone from the pit, he tore his clothes in distress.
He cried out, “The child is not; and I, whither shall I go?” (Genesis 37:30, KJV)
And in Genesis 42:22, Reuben reminded his brothers that he had warned them not to sin against Joseph.
This is important.
The Bible does not reduce Reuben's entire life to one act as though nothing else he ever did mattered.
He showed concern for Joseph.
He attempted to intervene.
He experienced anguish.
Yet those later actions did not reverse the recorded loss of his birthright.
Scripture also does not explicitly tell us the complete state of Reuben's heart before God at the end of his life.
We should not declare him eternally condemned, nor invent a repentance scene the Bible never records.
The text gives us a historical judgment concerning his preeminence, not a complete account of his eternal destiny.
And that distinction is essential for understanding the Gospel correctly.
Because losing a privilege is not the same thing as proving that God's mercy is unavailable.
Consequences are not proof that repentance is useless.
And a painful history is not proof that Jesus Christ cannot redeem a life.
Now consider something extraordinary.
In Deuteronomy 33:6, Moses says:
“Let Reuben live, and not die; and let not his men be few.” (KJV)
The tribe of Reuben was not erased from Israel.
Despite the loss of firstborn preeminence, Reuben's descendants remained among the tribes of God's covenant people.
And in Revelation 7:5, Reuben's tribe is named among the tribes in John's vision of the sealed servants of God.
That does not mean every individual descendant of Reuben was automatically saved, nor does it cancel the historical consequences pronounced in Genesis.
But it does show that Reuben's name was not simply wiped from the biblical story.
His loss of preeminence did not mean his descendants disappeared from the history of God's people.
And here, the story begins to open toward a greater hope.
Because the Bible is not ultimately the story of human beings successfully preserving their own honor.
It is the story of God's redemptive purpose unfolding through deeply flawed human history.
Consider Judah.
Judah was not morally spotless.
Genesis 38 records his own shameful conduct and his eventual acknowledgment of wrongdoing.
Yet Genesis 49:10 associates the scepter with Judah, and the New Testament identifies Jesus Christ as coming from Judah's line.
Revelation 5:5 calls Him:
“The Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David.” (KJV)
Think about the wonder of that.
The royal line of the Messiah did not emerge from a family history untouched by scandal.
It emerged from a family whose story included deception, rivalry, sexual sin, betrayal, grief, and broken relationships.
Yet God's promise did not collapse under the weight of human failure.
His redemptive purpose continued.
And at the center of that purpose stands Jesus Christ.
The One who never surrendered to temptation.
The One who never defiled what was holy.
The One who never used His position for selfish corruption.
The One who remained obedient to the Father.
Where Reuben failed to honor his father's household, Jesus perfectly honored His heavenly Father.
Where human beings have misused privilege, Christ humbled Himself in obedience.
Where our desires have so often ruled us, Jesus resisted temptation without sin.
Hebrews 4:15 declares that He was “in all points tempted like as we are, yet without sin.” (KJV)
And Philippians 2:8 says:
“And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.” (KJV)
Do you see the contrast?
Reuben possessed the status of firstborn but failed in a moment of grievous disobedience.
Jesus Christ, whom the New Testament calls the “firstborn among many brethren” in Romans 8:29, fulfilled His mission in perfect obedience.
The term πρωτότοκος (prōtotokos), meaning “firstborn,” is used in several New Testament passages to express Christ's unique supremacy and relationship to God's redemptive purposes.
Colossians 1:18 calls Jesus “the firstborn from the dead,” emphasizing His preeminence in the new creation.
And Hebrews 1:6 speaks of God's Firstborn in the context of the Son's exalted dignity.
These passages do not teach that Jesus is a created being. The same chapter of Colossians declares that all things were created through Him and for Him.
He is supreme over creation, not merely another creature within it.
Reuben lost his preeminence through sin.
Christ possesses preeminence in perfect righteousness.
And through His death and resurrection, sinners can receive something they could never earn through their own moral record.
Reconciliation with God.
Forgiveness.
Adoption.
New life.
An inheritance secured by grace.
Romans 8:16–17 says that believers are children of God and, as His children, heirs of God and joint-heirs with Christ.
Do not misunderstand that glorious promise.
It does not mean every lost opportunity will return.
It does not mean every damaged relationship will be restored exactly as it once was.
It does not mean repentance guarantees earthly prominence, financial success, or the recovery of a former position.
The Gospel promises something far deeper than the restoration of worldly status.
It promises that through faith in Jesus Christ, guilty sinners can be justified before God, reconciled to Him, and brought into His family.
That is greater than any birthright a human father could give.
And it was purchased at a cost we could never pay.
The blood of Jesus Christ.
Imagine standing before God with the complete record of your life exposed.
Every selfish ambition.
Every concealed betrayal.
Every unclean thought.
Every moment you knowingly resisted the truth.
Every excuse.
Every compromise.
Every failure.
No reputation to hide behind.
No ministry achievement to display as payment.
No religious performance sufficient to erase guilt.
Only the truth.
And then consider what the Gospel announces.
Romans 5:8:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” (KJV)
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had successfully repaired every consequence.
Not after we had become impressive enough to deserve acceptance.
Not after we had managed to rewrite our own history.
Christ died for sinners.
This is not cheap grace.
The cross does not minimize sin.
The cross reveals how serious sin is.
But it also reveals how astonishing God's mercy is.
Jesus did not come merely to make morally wounded people feel better about themselves.
He came to save sinners.
To reconcile the lost to God.
To deliver people from the dominion of sin.
To create a people who belong to Him.
To make possible the transformation we could never accomplish by self-effort alone.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
Notice those words.
“In Christ.”
That is where the promise rests.
Not in motivational thinking.
Not in pretending the past was harmless.
Not in declaring ourselves innocent.
But in union with the crucified and risen Savior.
And perhaps this is the moment you need to hear something that your shame has been drowning out.
You cannot go backward and become the person who never sinned.
But you can turn to the Savior who died for sinners.
You cannot force every person you wounded to trust you again.
But you can confess the truth, make appropriate amends, accept accountability, and begin walking in obedience.
You cannot demand that God restore every position you lost.
But you can entrust your future to the One who knows how to bring genuine redemption out of a broken life.
Your past must be faced honestly.
But it does not have to become your master.
Sin must be confessed.
But shame does not have to become your identity.
Consequences may remain.
But Christ's grace is not exhausted by their presence.
Perhaps you are reading this while carrying the memory of a failure that nobody else knows about.
Perhaps you are a husband who knows he has been emotionally unfaithful.
A wife who has allowed bitterness to poison her heart.
A young person secretly struggling with pornography.
A church worker who has learned to maintain a spiritual appearance while privately drifting from God.
A parent who cannot stop remembering the words spoken in anger.
Or someone who has been living with the consequences of a decision made many years ago.
You may feel as though the best part of your life is already behind you.
As though your usefulness ended when your reputation was damaged.
As though God could never receive someone who knew better and still chose wrongly.
But hear the words of Jesus in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
That invitation is not restricted to people with uncomplicated histories.
It is for sinners who come to Christ.
The tax collector.
The immoral.
The proud.
The religious hypocrite who finally stops pretending.
The exhausted believer who needs to repent and return.
The person who has fallen again and is finally ready to stop defending the fall.
Come to Him.
Not because sin is small.
But because His mercy is great.
Not because your actions had no consequences.
But because your guilt is not greater than the sufficiency of His sacrifice.
And do not confuse coming to Jesus with simply feeling emotional while reading an article.
A tear is not the same as repentance.
A comment is not the same as conversion.
The response Christ calls for is faith and repentance—a genuine turning to Him that bears fruit in a changed life.
If you need to confess a hidden sin, confess it to God.
If someone has been harmed, seek to make things right where possible and safe, without pressuring them to forgive you on your timetable.
If you are trapped in a destructive pattern, seek trustworthy pastoral guidance and appropriate professional help when needed.
If you are continuing in deliberate sin, do not use the language of grace as permission to remain there.
Romans 6:1–2 confronts that very distortion:
“Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid.” (KJV)
Grace is not permission to remain enslaved.
Grace calls us into the freedom of belonging to Jesus Christ.
And that freedom is not merely a feeling.
It is a new direction of life.
Maybe you have lost something because of your own choices.
Maybe you are still grieving what might have been.
Maybe the consequences are so visible that you cannot escape the reminder.
Then remember this.
Reuben's story is a warning about the seriousness of sin.
But the larger biblical story points us to a Savior whose power to redeem is greater than human failure.
You may not recover every earthly privilege.
But you can know the God who forgives.
You may not undo every wound.
But by His grace, you can stop creating new ones.
You may not be able to rewrite yesterday.
But in Christ, yesterday does not have the final authority over who you are becoming.
That is why we keep returning to the Gospel.
Not because every story ends with an easy earthly restoration.
But because Jesus Christ is worthy of our trust even when the road of repentance is costly.
Because the cross tells the truth about our sin while offering the hope of forgiveness.
Because the empty tomb declares that death itself did not defeat our Redeemer.
Because the Lord who calls us to holiness is also the Lord who gives grace to those who come to Him.
And because some of the most powerful testimonies are not stories of people who never fell.
They are stories of people who stopped hiding, surrendered to Jesus, and learned to walk in the light.
If this story has exposed something you have been hiding, I want to invite you into an honest moment.
Not a performance for strangers.
Not a public confession of details that should be handled privately and wisely.
Just an opportunity to acknowledge your need for God's mercy.
You can comment, “Lord, teach me to walk in the light.”
Or, if you are weary from fighting a spiritual battle, comment, “Pray for me. I'm still fighting.”
And if Christ has been restoring your life after a season of failure, consider sharing a testimony of His grace—without revealing anything that would harm another person's privacy.
Someone reading may need to know that repentance is possible.
Someone may need the courage to seek help.
Someone may need to hear that the way back to God is not through pretending, but through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that someone is a person you know.
A brother who has become distant from the faith.
A sister carrying hidden shame.
A friend who believes their worst mistake has disqualified them forever.
A family member who has been drifting away from the Lord.
Not as a lucky charm.
Not as a substitute for opening your Bible.

But as a reminder to return to Genesis 35, Genesis 49, 1 Chronicles 5, and the glorious promises of the Gospel whenever temptation whispers that obedience does not matter—or shame whispers that mercy is impossible.

And if you believe that sound biblical teaching, Gospel-centered encouragement, and serious discipleship should reach more people, I want to invite you to become part of what we are building through Gospel Warrior.
It is about pointing people to Jesus Christ, helping them understand Scripture, encouraging repentance and faith, and reminding wounded people that God's truth and mercy must never be separated.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment accessible to people who may be hungry for truth but unable to afford extensive Christian reading materials.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (KJV)
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not through guilt.
Not through pressure.
Not through the suggestion that your love for God can be measured by a payment.
But through willing generosity, if you believe this ministry is faithfully serving Christ and you want to help it continue.
You can still read, learn, pray, share, invite others, and make use of the free resources.
Your worth before God is not determined by your financial capacity.
And the grace of Jesus Christ is not for sale.
Because what matters most is not the growth of a page.
It is that more people encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
And now, before you leave, return with me one final time to the scene at Jacob's deathbed.
An aging father.
His sons gathered around him.
A firstborn standing among his brothers.
A privilege once held.
A boundary crossed.
A consequence pronounced.
“Unstable as water, thou shalt not excel.”
Those words should make every one of us examine our lives.
Not with self-righteousness.
Not with a desire to condemn Reuben from a comfortable distance.
But with trembling humility.
Because apart from God's grace, we are all capable of terrible choices.
And because none of us has obeyed perfectly enough to stand righteous before God on our own merit.
That is why we need Jesus.
Not merely as an inspiring example.
Not merely as a religious figure we admire.
But as Savior and Lord.
The spotless Lamb of God.
The risen King.
The One who calls sinners to repentance and grants forgiveness through His finished work.
The One whose grace does not excuse our darkness, but brings us into His marvelous light.
So do not wait until your heart becomes harder.
Do not wait until another secret becomes another wound.
Do not wait until the consequences become more severe.
Turn to Christ today.
And if you have already fallen, do not make the additional mistake of believing that hiding will heal you.
Come into the light.
Confess what must be confessed.
Turn from what must be abandoned.
Accept the consequences that must be faced.
Trust the Savior who alone can cleanse your conscience and make you new.
Let Reuben's loss warn you.
Let Christ's obedience humble you.
Let the cross draw you.
Let the resurrection give you hope.
And let the grace of God produce in you a life that increasingly reflects the One who saved you.
Because your greatest need is not to recover the throne you lost.
It is to bow before the King who never lost His righteousness.
You may never get back everything sin took from you, but in Jesus Christ, you can receive what sin could never give you: forgiveness, a new heart, and life with God.
